app.footer: The dataset is re-fetched from the official sources and re-checked by GitHub Actions (daily, and whenever the pipeline code changes); every number can be traced to its source file and checksum under “Methods & sources”.
app.lede: Wages in every economy are first converted into grams of gold; then we look at what those grams buy locally. All figures come from official publications — the World Bank, the International Labour Organization (ILOSTAT), the OECD and national statistical offices — and every source file is archived, traceable and recomputable.
app.stale: {n} sources were not updated in this run; their previous snapshots are used
app.title: How much gold is an hour of work worth — and what does that gold buy?
buys.aria: What a gram of gold buys, by economy
buys.col_diet: 1 g of gold = days of healthy diet
buys.note_consumption: International dollars = US-dollar price of 1 g of gold ÷ the economy’s price level of household consumption (purchasing power parity ÷ market exchange rate, World Bank WDI). It covers all household consumption, including housing and services. The international dollar is the unit of the International Comparison Program: it has the purchasing power of a US dollar in the United States.
buys.note_diet: Healthy diet: the World Bank Food Prices for Nutrition cost of a healthy diet for one person for one day (local currency, current prices). It covers food only, and takes the cheapest available option in each food group — not a typical household’s shopping basket.
buys.sub: Local gold prices are the US-dollar price × the exchange rate, so in dollars a gram is worth the same everywhere; but converted into local currency, the same gram buys more where prices are lower. The differences in this step are the differences in price levels.

gold.note_concepts: Concepts can differ a lot: in this dataset an ILOSTAT survey’s average monthly wage is {min}–{max} times OECD’s full-time-equivalent average wage for the same economy and year ({n} pairs), so rankings across different concepts should be read with care; the data table lists the other figures of the same year.
gold.note_fx: The official rate is checked each year against the factor the World Bank used to convert that year’s GDP; agreeing within ×/÷{mf} shows they are in the same currency unit, not that they are the same rate (fiscal-year or multiple exchange rates make them differ). Differences of 0.5% or more are listed in the tooltip.
gold.note_fx_gap: The official rate is checked each year against the factor the World Bank used to convert that year’s GDP; agreeing within ×/÷{mf} shows they are in the same currency unit, not that they are the same rate (fiscal-year or multiple exchange rates make them differ; in this chart for {year} they differ by up to {pct}%). Differences of 0.5% or more are listed in the tooltip.
gold.note_median: The dots are medians from the same survey as the bar, drawn only where that survey also publishes a median.
gold.note_order: Which wage figure is used: OECD’s full-time-equivalent average wage (hourly via OECD’s usual weekly hours of full-time employees) → ILOSTAT average wages covering all employees nationwide (where only monthly figures exist, converted with the same survey’s weekly hours) → national statistical offices’ own figures (coverage as they state it) → ILOSTAT figures with limited coverage (e.g. urban only, private sector only, full-time only). Where an economy’s main figure differs from the previous year’s, the tooltip says so.
gold.note_sources: Each economy’s measure and the publisher’s notes are in the tooltip and the data table. Gold: World Bank Pink Sheet monthly averages, averaged over the year; exchange rate: World Bank WDI annual average official rate.
gold.sub: Wage ÷ ({year} average gold price ÷ 31.1034768 g per troy ounce × that year’s average exchange rate). This is the same as converting the wage into US dollars at the market rate and dividing by the dollar price of a gram of gold.
gold.title_hour: ① Work → gold: grams of gold per hour of work ({year})
gold.title_month: ① Work → gold: grams of gold per month of work ({year})
how.missing_hour: No hourly figure of the same concept for {year}: {list}.
how.missing_month: No monthly figure of the same concept for {year}: {list}.
how.note: “Healthy diet” is the World Bank Food Prices for Nutrition “cost of a healthy diet”: the cheapest locally available foods that together make up a healthy diet from six food groups, for one person for one day. “—” means the input could not be shown to be in the same currency unit as the World Bank’s local-currency series, or is missing (reasons under “Methods & sources”). International dollars: converted at the purchasing power parity of household consumption.
how.ruler_body: Local gold prices here are the US-dollar gold price × the exchange rate, so at any given time the ratio of two economies’ “grams of gold” equals the ratio of their wages converted at market exchange rates — gold does not remove the exchange rate. What changes the picture is step ②: the same gram of gold buys more where prices are lower. In step ③ the gold cancels out, so the result does not depend on measuring in gold at all.
how.step1_f_hour: = hourly wage ÷ local gold price per gram (US-dollar gold price × exchange rate)
how.step1_f_month: = monthly wage ÷ local gold price per gram (US-dollar gold price × exchange rate)
how.step2_f: = local gold price per gram ÷ cost of a healthy diet for one person for one day
how.step2_v: days of a healthy diet per gram
how.step3_f_hour: = hourly wage ÷ diet cost: the gold cancels out
how.step3_f_month: = monthly wage ÷ diet cost: the gold cancels out
how.step3_v_hour: days of a healthy diet per hour of work
how.step3_v_month: days of a healthy diet per month of work
how.sub_hour: One calculation for every economy: how many grams of gold an hour’s wage buys, then how much a gram of gold buys locally; multiplied together, that is what the hour of work buys.
how.sub_month: One calculation for every economy: how many grams of gold a month’s wage buys, then how much a gram of gold buys locally; multiplied together, that is what the month of work buys.

m.c_continuity: A change between two years of one source is compared with the change in nominal household consumption per head and in nominal GDP per head (World Bank local-currency values ÷ population); where it deviates from every available yardstick by more than OECD’s same-concept average wages have deviated from the same yardstick over as many years or fewer (against household consumption per head: {hfce}; against GDP per head: {gdp}), the notes say “the concept or scale may have changed” and the history lines break there; between two years whose notes on what the figure measures differ, or across a noted break, only a difference beyond ×/÷{tf} is noted.
m.c_diet: The “cheapest healthy diet” covers food only, and takes the cheapest available foods, so it is not what a typical household actually spends; housing, health, education and social insurance — large items for living standards — are not in the food basket; read it together with “What costs more where” and purchasing power parity.
m.c_excluded_notes: Records ILOSTAT notes as “real values” (at some base year’s prices), as not an average or median wage (such as a minimum wage), as in a time unit that does not match the indicator, or with the observation status “unreliable” are not used; other notes (such as “use with caution”) are shown verbatim.
m.c_ilostat: ILOSTAT compiles each economy’s official sources (labour force surveys, establishment surveys, administrative records), so concepts differ between economies. The publisher’s notes on each record (e.g. urban only, private sector only, net of tax, full-time only) are shown verbatim in tooltips and tables; records whose notes say they cover only part of the employees are labelled “limited coverage”. Order of preference: OECD → ILOSTAT records covering all employees nationwide → national statistical offices’ own figures (coverage as they state it) → ILOSTAT records with limited coverage.
m.c_intl_dollar: International dollars are the unit of the World Bank’s International Comparison Program: by construction, an international dollar buys in any economy what a US dollar buys in the United States. That is a convention of the unit, not a choice of this site.
m.c_median: An average wage is usually higher than the median (a few high earners pull the average up). The dots are the median published by the same survey as the bar; where the bar comes from OECD, or the survey has no median, none is drawn, so that figures from different sources are not read as one distribution.
m.c_monthly_view: Comparing monthly wages needs no assumption about hours; comparing hourly wages depends on hours data, so economies without hours of the same concept appear only in the monthly view.
m.c_nso: Besides the international sources, two national statistical offices’ own releases are read: China’s National Bureau of Statistics (average wages of urban non-private units, urban private units and large enterprises; migrant workers’ average monthly income; enterprise employees’ weekly hours) and the US Bureau of Labor Statistics (average hourly earnings of private non-farm employees). They go through the same rules as every other source and appear only for their own economy; other national offices’ releases are not read in this version.
m.c_same_year: All economies use the same reference year’s wages, exchange rates, gold price and prices; economies without a verifiable wage for that year are not in the charts. The top of the page lists the G20 members without data (with “All economies”, the focus economies without data).
m.c_time_units: Scale and time unit: one survey’s monthly and hourly figures, converted with that survey’s measured hours, should differ by no more than ×/÷{tf} (the logarithmic midpoint of the week-to-month ratio {ug}), and monthly ÷ hourly must lie between 1 and 744 hours; where the survey has no hours, they are converted with the median of other sources’ weekly hours that year (OECD’s usual hours of full-time employees included) and are judged wrong only from ×/÷{ug}. The same kind of figure (mean or median) from different sources: within ×/÷{tf} they confirm each other; at ×/÷{ug} (a whole week-to-month factor) or more, one of them has a wrong unit or scale; in between, a difference of concept and a wrong time unit cannot be told apart, so the figures are kept and said to be unconfirmed. A month’s pay above a year’s GDP per head, or below a week’s household consumption per head, is taken as an unknown time unit or scale, and none of that survey’s figures in that time unit is used. Only another source can confirm a figure’s scale (one survey’s monthly and hourly figures come from the same data); when figures disagree and the data cannot tell which is wrong, none of them is used.
m.c_translation: The site’s text is available in several languages. The translations were produced with an AI model and cross-checked in a second pass, not by professional translators. Text quoted from publishers (ILOSTAT’s English notes, NBS’s Chinese releases) stays in its original language, and economies’ names come from your browser’s own list of names.
m.checks: Cross-checks (run on every refresh; if any fails, no new data is published)
m.concepts: Differences in concept to keep in mind
m.excl_joins: Wages and diet costs are then joined to a proven exchange rate or PPP: an ILOSTAT wage ÷ the exchange rate (or ÷ the PPP) must match ILOSTAT’s own US-dollar (or PPP) value; the diet cost in local currency ÷ its PPP value must match the PPP; OECD’s constant-price national-currency wage ÷ its PPP-dollar value must match the PPP of the base year; the currency a national statistical office states must match the proven currency.
m.excl_rates: Exchange rates and PPPs are proven only by the World Bank’s own data: the official rate against “GDP in local currency ÷ in US dollars”, the PPP against “household consumption in local currency ÷ in international dollars”, within ×/÷{mf}; where the World Bank lacks these, the 2021 PPP is checked against the ICP 2021 price level of household consumption (which has no currency unit) × the official rate; a year with nothing to check carries over an adjacent year’s check (a value that moves by no more than ×/÷{mf} cannot have changed unit); a year whose identity fails although its value moves by less than ×/÷{mf} each year from a proven year is in the same unit — the inconsistency has another, unknown cause — and is not used either.
m.excl_rule: Inputs that cannot be proven are not used. The rules look only at the numbers and name no country; each record’s kind, reason and numbers are below.
m.excl_units: Every number divides one institution’s figure (a wage) by another’s (an exchange rate, a PPP, a diet cost), so both must be in the same currency unit. Since 2000 (the first year of these data), the smallest factor of any non-par currency redenomination or euro changeover has been 1.42 (Latvia joining the euro in 2014), so within these years “differ by no more than ×/÷{mf}” proves the same unit — though not the same number.
m.f_gold: Local gold price (local currency per gram) = the year’s average gold price (US$ per troy ounce) ÷ 31.1034768 × the year’s average exchange rate (local currency per US$)
m.f_ilo: ILOSTAT economies with only monthly wages: hourly wage = monthly wage ÷ (the same survey’s weekly hours actually worked × 52 ÷ 12); without hours from the same survey, the figure is used for the monthly view only
m.f_nso: National statistical offices’ annual wages: hourly wage = annual wage ÷ 12 ÷ (the office’s own weekly hours × 52 ÷ 12), the hours averaged over the year’s archived months (at least 6, otherwise no hourly figure) — currently China’s NBS (average weekly hours of enterprise employees)
m.f_oecd: OECD data: hourly wage = full-time-equivalent average annual wage ÷ (usual weekly hours of full-time employees × 52)
m.f_step1: ① Gold per hour of work (g) = hourly wage (local currency) ÷ local gold price
m.f_step2_diet: ② Days of healthy diet per gram of gold = local gold price ÷ cost of a healthy diet for one person for one day (local currency)
m.f_step2_intl: ② Purchasing power of 1 g of gold (international $) = US-dollar gold price per gram ÷ price level of household consumption (PPP ÷ exchange rate)
m.f_step3: ③ Hourly wage at PPP = hourly wage ÷ household-consumption PPP = ① × ② (the pipeline checks this identity for every record)
m.src_note: Snapshot = the raw bytes the publisher returned, unmodified; the SHA-256 lets you verify a file has not been altered. Refresh: daily at 07:23 UTC and whenever the pipeline code changes; it can also be run from the repository’s Actions page (“data-refresh” → “Run workflow”). This table lists only the files read to build this dataset; older snapshots stay in the repository for audit. Raw-file links point to the branch the site was built from ({branch}).
m.sub: Every number can be traced to a file an official publisher released. The pipeline code, the raw snapshots and the check results are all in the repository.

ps.note_cols: Columns: Consumption = household consumption, i.e. the final consumption of households and non-profit institutions serving households as a whole; Food = food and non-alcoholic beverages; Housing = housing, water, electricity, gas and other fuels. The Housing, Health and Education columns use ICP’s “actual individual consumption” concept, which includes what governments and non-profit institutions provide to households, not only what households pay themselves.
ps.note_year: This chart uses ICP 2021 as published; the yearly overall price level used in the other sections comes from World Bank WDI, and the two can differ slightly for 2021 because of revisions. Prices and exchange rates have changed since 2021, so this is not a precise picture of today’s gaps (for the yearly overall level see “② Gold → goods”, in international dollars).
ps.spread: Across the {n} economies in ICP 2021 that are on the World Bank’s list of economies, the middle half of food and non-alcoholic beverage price levels spans a factor of {food} (75th ÷ 25th percentile); for {services}.
ps.spread_conclusion: Goods that can be traded across borders, like food, are priced more alike across economies than local services.
ps.sub: World Bank International Comparison Program (ICP), 2021 benchmark: goods and services of the same specifications are priced in every economy and converted at market exchange rates. ICP publishes the price level index with the world average = 100; here you can also compare against any economy.

real.note: Log scale. US dollars at the market rate = grams of gold × the dollar price of a gram, because every local gold price is the dollar price × the exchange rate. The international dollar has the purchasing power of a US dollar in the United States (the ICP convention), so for the United States the two values coincide.
real.sub_hour: For each economy, the same hourly wage converted two ways: at the market exchange rate into US dollars (grey — the same as measuring in grams of gold) and at purchasing power parity into international dollars (blue — local prices taken into account). The distance between the two dots is how much local prices narrow or widen the gap.
real.sub_month: For each economy, the same monthly wage converted two ways: at the market exchange rate into US dollars (grey — the same as measuring in grams of gold) and at purchasing power parity into international dollars (blue — local prices taken into account). The distance between the two dots is how much local prices narrow or widen the gap.

ruler.callout_down: From {y0} to {y1} the annual average gold price fell from US${a0} to US${a1} per troy ounce. A wage measured in grams of gold rises whenever gold falls or rises more slowly than the wage, even if what the wage buys locally has not changed.
ruler.callout_up: From {y0} to {y1} the annual average gold price rose from US${a0} to US${a1} per troy ounce (×{r}). A wage measured in grams of gold falls whenever gold rises faster than the wage, even if what the wage buys locally has not changed.
ruler.gold_note: World Bank Pink Sheet monthly averages (per the workbook’s description, averages of daily spot prices since June 2025, of London afternoon fixings before). The benchmark price is published in US dollars.
ruler.gold_title: Gold price, US$ per troy ounce (monthly average, log scale)
ruler.hist_breaks: Lines are broken, so that two figures that may not be comparable are not joined, where: the publisher notes a break in series or a change of coverage (such as ILOSTAT’s “Break in series” or a national statistical office’s “comparable basis”); ILOSTAT’s notes on what the figure measures change; or the change between two points of one source, compared with the change in nominal household consumption and GDP per head over the same years (World Bank local-currency values ÷ population), is out of line with both by more than OECD’s same-concept average wages have been over as many years (against household consumption per head: {bounds}), or cannot be checked.
ruler.hist_note: Each year’s monthly wage is converted with that year’s average gold price and average exchange rate.
ruler.hist_rule: One series per economy: among OECD’s full-time-equivalent wage and each ILOSTAT survey’s average monthly wage with at least 3 years, the one with the most years not restricted in coverage.
ruler.hist_title: Average monthly wage in grams of gold (annual, log scale)
ruler.isolated: Isolated points (broken on both sides) are drawn as dots.
ruler.local_none: There is no year in which all focus economies have a verified exchange rate.
ruler.local_note: Annual average gold price × annual average official exchange rate, as an index with {year} = 100 (the first year in which every focus economy has one). A steeper line means gold rose faster in that currency — partly because the currency fell against the US dollar.
ruler.local_title: Gold price in each economy’s own currency (index, log scale)
ruler.no_history: No series of at least 3 verified years from one source (OECD or ILOSTAT average monthly wage): {list}.
ruler.prompt: Pick focus economies to compare the gold price in their own currencies and their average wage in grams of gold over time:
ruler.sub: Pricing in gold strips out a currency’s own depreciation, but the gold price itself swings widely: the same wage in grams of gold can double or halve within a few years.
